title: Qualitative Insights From Public Interviews in the United Kingdom on the Acceptability of Risk-Based Eligibility Criteria for Lung Cancer Screening

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Qualitative Insights From Public Interviews in the United Kingdom on the Acceptability of Risk-Based Eligibility Criteria for Lung Cancer Screening》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · hex70937-sec-0070-p1】Lung cancer remains the primary cause of cancer‐related deaths globally [1]. Screening with low‐dose computed tomography (LDCT) significantly reduces mortality among high‐risk individuals [2, 3], where the benefit‐risk ratio is most favourable [4]. Many countries have introduced targeted lung cancer screening programmes, with eligibility largely driven by age and tobacco smoking history but approaches to risk‐based selection vary. In the United States (US), eligibility requires meeting categorical thresholds: age (50–80 years), ≥ 20 pack‐years smoking history, and smoking within the past 15 years [5].

【Introduction · hex70937-sec-0070-p2】In the United Kingdom (UK), national roll‐out of lung cancer screening was recommended in 2022 [6], with the national English programme aiming for full coverage by 2030. Individuals are invited to an initial telephone‐based lung health check to assess their lung cancer risk if they are aged between 55 and 74 and have ever been recorded as smoking by their primary care practice. Eligibility for low‐dose CT lung cancer screening is determined using multivariable risk models [7, 8, 9] evidenced to be more sensitive and efficient at identifying who to screen than categorical criteria [10, 11]. These models (Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial Model 2012; Liverpool Lung Project‐v28–10) calculate individual risk scores using age, tobacco smoking, and additional factors such as personal/family cancer history, respiratory disease, environmental/occupational exposures, race/ethnicity, education level (as an individual‐level proxy measure of socioeconomic group) and body mass index (BMI). Each risk factor contributes to the score according to its coefficient, with smoking history weighted more heavily than others. Those who meet or exceed a specified threshold are eligible to be invited for low‐dose CT screening.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Qualitative Insights From Public Interviews in the United Kingdom on the Acceptability of Risk-Based Eligibility Criteria for Lung Cancer Screening》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Public and Patient Involvement · hex70937-sec-0120-p1】The research team sought the views of eight public and patient representatives with lung cancer experience (either personally affected or being a carer) during study conception. They endorsed the research objectives, helped to develop relevant participant‐facing interview questions and gave feedback on the appropriateness of the design, agreeing that in‐depth interviews would best capture perceptions of the acceptability of risk‐based eligibility criteria.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Qualitative Insights From Public Interviews in the United Kingdom on the Acceptability of Risk-Based Eligibility Criteria for Lung Cancer Screening》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Results · hex70937-sec-0140-p2】Themes were organised into three categories (1): How acceptable are the risk‐based eligibility criteria for lung screening? (2) What does it mean to be eligible or ineligible for lung screening? and (3) Recommendations for communication about the risk‐based criteria. Theme descriptions are supported by illustrative quotes (including participants' gender: (M) Male; (F) Female, ethnicity: (W) White; (M) Mixed/Multiple; (A) Asian; (B) Black; (O) Other, smoking group: (C) Current; (F) Former; (N) Never) with further evidence in Supporting Information: File 4. Detailed comparative analysis by smoking status was not undertaken, as the study aimed to generate in‐depth insights into how participants interpreted the eligibility criteria and formed views on acceptability. Associations between smoking status and acceptability were examined in the parallel survey. A brief post‐hoc exploratory analysis of the qualitative data found no consistent differences in views expressed according to smoking status, however, these findings are purely descriptive and based on small numbers of participants who have never smoked (N = 5).

【Results · hex70937-sec-0140-p1】Of 4876 individuals who completed the online questionnaire, 3093 (63.4%) agreed to be contacted to take part in an interview. One hundred and twenty were initially invited to take part in the interview study and 90 (75% of 120 invited) expressed their interest to participate. Of the first 33 who were identified as eligible, 28 (84.9%) individuals (Mean age = 57 years, SD = 8, range: 45–77) (14 females) participated (Mean duration of interview = 35 min, SD = 5, range: 25–47) (Table 1). The remaining participants were unable to be contacted. A sample of 28 was considered appropriate as it aligns with current qualitative research practice providing sufficiently rich and varied accounts to support an in‐depth thematic analysis and achieve sufficient information power. Consistent with the five dimensions outlined in Malterud, Siersma and Guassora's information power approach [36], the sample size of 28 provided sufficient information power due to (1) highly focused study aims (2), purposive sampling to ensure diversity of perspectives (3), utilisation of an established theoretical framework, the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability, to guide data collection and analysis (4), detailed, rich interview content and (5) in‐depth focused thematic analysis.
